name: Diego Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for doing this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, so no AI companies, employers, unions or government behind us, and what you tell me stays anonymous. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I process travel insurance claims for Wayfare Cover, a direct insurer, mostly from home three days a week and in the office on Tuesdays and Thursdays. It's cancelled flights, lost bags, people who broke an ankle skiing and need their hospital bill paid. I read the story, match it to the policy wording, request receipts and either approve small ones or send them up.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the part you enjoy, and what's the part that drains you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the puzzle of it, and I've got a whole set of AI prompts that turn a messy email into a neat claim summary in seconds. The draining part is that I'm fast but sloppy. Last month I approved a lost-camera claim that had an exclusion for items left in a car, and Hassan, my team leader, had to claw it back. That one still makes my ears go hot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. That would be a bit disappointing, to be honest. I've put a lot of evenings into learning these tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work that the tools are still worth it, because they are; they save me twenty minutes a day. Online I'd probably admit the hype was overblown and that the boring stuff is still boring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be okay. My edge is that I already use AI more than anyone else on the team, so a small change still favours me a bit. What wouldn't change is that I need to stop missing exclusions, and no tool fixes that for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Hassan if I can write up my prompts as a team guide, because that gets my name noticed for something good. I'd do the insurance certificate course that the company pays for, the entry-level one, because my weakness is policy wording, not speed. And I'd keep the three months I've got saved and add to it slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A little flat, like a film that didn't have the ending it promised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's weighing on you in that world, outside AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, honestly. I share a flat with two friends, the rent's fine split three ways, and Wayfare's busy because everyone's travelling again. The only real worry is being the guy who keeps getting claims clawed back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay at Wayfare in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay, I think. It's a decent first proper job and I'd rather get good at it than jump. Maybe in two years I'd look at the bigger insurers in town, where the pay's a bit better.

say: I'd tell colleagues the **tools still save** me twenty minutes a day.
Online I'd admit the **hype was overblown** and boring work stays boring.
think: Using AI more than anyone gives me a **small edge** even in a quiet world.
My real gap is **missing exclusions**, and no tool fixes that for me.
do: Write up my **AI prompts** as a team guide and offer it to my team leader.
Take the company-paid **insurance certificate** course to learn policy wording.
Keep adding slowly to my **three months** of savings.
feel: Calm, and a little **flat**, like a film without the promised ending.
S0.quote: My edge is that I already use AI more than anyone else on the team, so a small change still favours me a bit.
fieldNote: He's **calm because secure enough**: cheap shared rent, busy employer, no dependants.
He names his own **sloppiness** honestly and sees training, not tech, as the fix.
A tinge of **disappointment** shows how much he's invested in AI.

steps.text: Write a team guide from his claim summary prompts
Take the company-paid entry insurance certificate course
Keep the Wayfare job and add slowly to savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is the one I actually expect. It's already starting at Wayfare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it straight: the work's changing, so let's make sure the people doing it now get the new jobs, not just consultants. I'd post that firms saving money with AI should pay into retraining funds. I believe that, it's not just a line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm in a weird spot. My job as it is now is exactly what gets automated: reading emails, matching wording, asking for receipts. But I'm also the person on the team who already knows how to run the tools, so I'm hoping to jump from doing claims to checking what the machine did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've already put my hand up to test the new triage system Wayfare's trialling in January, so I'd lean into that hard. I'd ask to be trained on fraud flags, because that's where the human checking will stay longest. I'd join the union too, honestly, because I want the people who can't jump to have someone fighting for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited, with an itch in the back of my head that says I'm not as good as I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be fine, but you also said you might be out. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair question. I'd be fine if the testing turns into a job. If they decide the testing role needs someone with three years' experience, then I'm just a junior who's slow on exclusions, and I'd be out with everyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the team would you think about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Margaret. She's been on the travel desk eleven years, she's brilliant at wording, and she hates computers. In a world like this I'd want to sit with her and swap: I teach her the tool, she teaches me the exclusions.

say: I'd argue current staff, **not consultants**, should get the new roles.
I'd post that firms saving with AI should fund **retraining**, and I mean it.
think: My current job is **exactly what goes**: emails, wording, receipts.
I hope to jump from doing claims to **checking the machine**, but it's not certain.
do: Test Wayfare's **new triage system** in the January trial.
Ask for training on **fraud flags**, where human checks stay longest.
**Join the union** so colleagues who can't switch have backing.
feel: Mostly **excited**, with an itch that I'm not as good as I think.
S1.quote: I'm also the person on the team who already knows how to run the tools, so I'm hoping to jump from doing claims to checking what the machine did.
fieldNote: He sees himself as **both exposed and positioned**, and admits the plan could fail.
His **progressive streak** shows in joining the union for others, not himself.
The **skill swap** idea with an older colleague is his most concrete and generous plan.

steps.text: Volunteer for the January trial of Wayfare's claim triage system
Ask for fraud flag training to move into checking roles
Join the finance workers' union this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, two years. That changes the game. Even the checking job I was aiming for doesn't last in that one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it publicly, plainly: this is too fast for people to adapt on their own, so governments need income support ready before it lands. I'd sign every petition going. I'd be loud about it because the people on my team who aren't techy would be hit first and hardest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it means my desk goes, probably inside the two years, and the clever-with-tools thing buys me maybe six months. But I'm twenty-seven with no kids and a cheap flat. I can move faster than almost anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd sit down and work out which jobs are hands-on and need people for at least the next five years. Electrician keeps coming up, and there's an adult apprenticeship at the college near my mum's. I'd keep Wayfare as long as it lasts, save everything above rent and food, and start the apprenticeship as soon as they'd take me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wired. Scared, but in a way that makes me move, not freeze.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The card says robots for hands-on work come three years later. Does that matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The robots part is what makes the electrician plan make sense. If thinking AI comes first and hands-on robots three years later, then I get maybe five years of wiring work before that catches up too. Five years earning is better than two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you have to explain this to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum. She'd ask why I'm throwing away an office job she was proud of. I'd tell my mum the office job was already gone, I just saw it first.

say: I'd push publicly for **income support** ready before it lands.
I'd sign every **petition**, because non-techy colleagues get hit first.
think: My desk goes **within two years**, and tool skills buy maybe six months.
Being **27 with no kids** and cheap rent means I can move fast.
do: Apply for the **adult electrician apprenticeship** at the college near my mum's.
Keep Wayfare while it lasts and **save everything** above rent and food.
**Sign petitions** for income support before AGI lands.
feel: **Wired** and scared, in a way that makes me move.
S2.quote: I'd tell my mum the office job was already gone, I just saw it first.
fieldNote: Even his **adaptive edge** fails here, and he says so plainly.
He used the **three-year robot gap** to pick a trade, which was the sharpest reasoning so far.
His freedom from **dependants** keeps him at anxious, not alarmed.

steps.text: Apply for the adult electrician apprenticeship near his mum's
Save everything above rent and food while Wayfare lasts
Sign petitions for income support before AGI arrives
Leave Wayfare once the apprenticeship takes him

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to be smart about it rather than just quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly, the same: income support, retraining funds, and make the firms pay into them. I'd also say to anyone younger than me, start learning a second thing now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd ride the AI wave at Wayfare for two or three years first, then switch into a trade with savings behind me instead of starting broke. Before that I'd be the guy running the new systems, earning a bit more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push for the triage tester role straight away and ask for a pay rise once I'm doing it. I'd start evening classes in electrical basics in year two, so I'm not starting from zero. By year four I'd want around eight months saved and an apprenticeship lined up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kind of good, honestly. Like I'm playing a game I understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong with being this confident?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd catch myself and remember the exclusions thing. I'm not as sharp as I like to think, and that's how I'd end up the last one out instead of the first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you tell first about the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hassan, probably. He's my team leader and he's been decent. I'd tell him early, so he can plan, and I'd want him to put in a word for me with the college.

say: I'd keep pushing for **firms to fund** retraining and income support.
I'd tell younger people to **learn a second thing** now.
think: I'd **ride the AI wave** at Wayfare for two or three years first.
Then switch to a trade with **savings behind me** instead of starting broke.
do: Go for the **triage tester** role and ask for a pay rise.
Start **evening electrical classes** in year two.
Reach **eight months saved** before an apprenticeship in year four.
feel: Kind of good, **in control**, like a game I understand.
S3.quote: I'd ride the AI wave at Wayfare for two or three years first, then switch into a trade with savings behind me instead of starting broke.
fieldNote: With time, he turns the threat into a **two-stage plan**: tools first, trade second.
He catches his own **overconfidence** when prompted, which is a healthy check.
His mood is **uneasy, not anxious**, because he sees control over timing.

steps.text: Take the triage tester role and ask for a pay rise
Start evening classes in electrical basics in year two
Build savings to eight months before switching careers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's long enough that I'd probably be a different person by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same things, but I'd also say we can't use ten years as an excuse to do nothing. Ten years is how long it takes to build proper training systems, not how long we can wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be pretty relaxed. I'd have time to get good at claims, get into the AI side, and maybe go to college part-time. There's time to do it in order instead of in a rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the insurance certificate this year and the next level after that. I'd move into the AI operations side at Wayfare. I'd probably go for a part-time degree in data or something near it, paid by the company if I can get it. The trade would be a backup plan, not the main one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Optimistic, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the catch with ten years, for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't really see one, honestly. I'd want to buy a place with my own name on it before thirty-five, and I'd have the time to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the trade is a backup. Would it still need to be ready by the end?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, fair. If I'm honest, the AI checking side might vanish at the same time as AGI, so in year nine I'd still need the trade. I'd keep the electrician idea alive, maybe do the first course anyway.

say: I'd warn that **ten years** is for building training systems, not waiting.
I'd keep backing **retraining funds** paid for by the firms.
think: I'd be **pretty relaxed**, with time to do things in order.
The **AI checking side** might vanish at AGI, so I still need a backup.
do: Finish the **insurance certificate** and the next level after it.
Move into **AI operations** at Wayfare and seek a part-time degree.
Take a first **electrical course** anyway as a backup.
S4.quote: Ten years is how long it takes to build proper training systems, not how long we can wait.
fieldNote: He's **calm** with a decade, but still keeps a hands-on backup in view.
Home ownership shows up as his **personal goal** for the first time.
He's clear that the **AI checking role** is temporary, even in the slow world.

steps.text: Finish the insurance certificate and its next level
Move into the AI operations team at Wayfare
Buy his own flat before age thirty-five

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Not for me so much, I'd scramble and probably land somewhere. It's colleagues like Margaret, who've been brilliant at this for years and would have nothing to land on. What would help is income support that's ready before it happens, and apprenticeships for adults that don't pay like they're for sixteen-year-olds.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether being good with AI tools is the same as being good at the job. It isn't. I'm the best on the team with the tools and one of the worst at the actual insurance, and I think people mix those up.

headlineQuote: I'm the best on the team with the tools and one of the worst at the actual insurance, and I think people mix those up.
portrait: Diego is a **27-year-old** travel claims clerk at Wayfare Cover, quick with AI but weak on policy wording.
He shares a **cheap flat** with two friends and has about three months saved.
He's **progressive** and joins the union for colleagues less able to switch than him.
His plans move from **testing AI tools** to an electrician apprenticeship as the scenarios get faster.
He's honest that **tool skill** and real insurance skill are not the same thing.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, mainly for long-serving colleagues with nothing to land on.
whatWouldHelp: **Income support** ready in advance, and adult apprenticeships with **decent pay**.
